summary: A state-built tower from about 1926 on Cheat Mountain with a 7x7 steel cab; standing but missing stairs and cab roof, no longer safe to climb, with a repeater beside it.

access.note: Forest hiking access: a gate, then a walk of the last 3/4 mile; the tower is not enclosed or fenced

visit.trail_note: Gate, then a 3/4-mile walk to the tower. Wikipedia says the tower is no longer safe to climb.

events.note: Built by the State of West Virginia circa 1926 (NHLR); a telephone-linked tower on Cheat Mountain is already reported in October 1926
Wikipedia: the tower has been on the summit since at least 1939, citing a 1939 Forest Service map
Road and related improvements at the fire tower were among projects listed in 1960
Photo caption on the NHLR shows the watchman's cabin remaining in October 2008
June 2010 Forest Service decision approved the Barton Knob Repeater Project, whose work list included removing the existing fire tower
Radio repeater installed by May 2012 adjacent to the tower; the tower was not removed
As of September 2016, Wikipedia describes the tower as abandoned and no longer safe to climb
NHLR visit report, April 18, 2017: bottom three flights of stairs gone, part of the floor gone, cab roof and windows gone; unstaffed

corrections.current: The tower still stands, but its cab is gone (FFLA).
corrections.proposed: The tower still stands, but its lower stairs are gone and the cab has lost its roof and windows (NHLR, 2017 visit).
corrections.why: The NHLR says the cab is missing its roof and the 2017 visit found the windows gone too; it does not say the cab itself is gone.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: NHLR gives circa 1926 and a 1926 newspaper item shows a tower already on Cheat Mountain. Wikipedia only says since at least 1939, citing a 1939 Forest Service map. The 1926 date is kept, and the 1939 figure is a later lower bound.
FFLA says the cab is gone; the NHLR register text says the cab is missing its roof, and its 2017 visit found the windows gone too. The NHLR account is followed.

notes_for_editor: Build date (circa 1926) rests on NHLR and one 1926 newspaper item; Wikipedia's 1939 is a weaker later bound. Condition is from a single 2017 NHLR visit and Wikipedia's 2016 status. The repeater project was approved in 2010 and the tower was not removed (Wikipedia). The Reddit and FFLA items were not used: a 1988 transfer to the Forest Service is unverified. Access: hiking via a gate and 3/4-mile walk; no climbing.
